The Jam/J. Geils Band/Van Halen/The Specials/Joe Jackson
Holland

A GOOD LINE up, huh? You bet. But as any of the 50,000 who came along to the eleventh Pink Pop Festival would have told you, it's quite a trek to the little town of Geleen in the most south easterly part of Holland. Since Netherlands Railways didn't run any extra trains for this capacity crowd, it was no surprise that sardine-sized fans fell out of the carriages only to find that they'd missed one or two of the bands; I got there for Joe Jackson.
In fine vocal form, Joe sports pillar box red drapes — every inch the spiv. Brash as usual, he launches into 'On Your Radio', followed by a couple of new ones. "You don't mind new ones do ya?" he shouts. The response is pretty non-committal; Jackson is cheesed off, does he ever smile?
'Look Sharp' and the new single, Jimmy Cliff's 'The Harder They Come', loosen up the crowd, finally really warming to 'One More Time' and 'Is She Really Going Out With Him?'. The latter has been re-worked (too much airplay?) and includes some subtle harmonies, but lacks the stamina which put it in the charts last year.
Once again our own John Peel was master of ceremonies. And he actually played some music inbetween enlightening the audience on the virtues of Kenny Dalglish and reprimanding the West Ham supporters who had chanted outside his room the previous night.
Now putting the Specials on at Pink Pop would be like expecting Sham 69 to play at Reading without a riot. 2 Tone fever is not exactly rampant in Holland, black and white checks being somewhat drowned in a sea of denim. After all, Pink Pop is to Holland what Knebworth is to Britain — head bashing, beer-swigging good fun. Good fun, that is, for everyone except the Specials. Much of the set was bland, lacking the usual vitality.
But let's be fair, 20 feet up on stage front of 50,000 ain't the local palais. Ska seemed a million miles away, and for one ghastly moment there was a hint that the Specials had been trading riffs with Van Halen backstage. The band made no bones about how they felt — they just weren't enjoying the set. They ploughed on, further aggravating the crowd. "This is our new single, 'Rat Race'. "It's sold 12 copies in Holland you bastards," said frontman Dammers. 'Too Much Too Young' and 'Message To Rudy' prompted some response, but it was too late for a resurrection.
By way of a contrast, Van Halen won before they even started, and the fact that Alex and Edward Van Halen were once from the land of tulips had very little to do with it. As the band played tracks from their 'Women And Children First' album an aeroplane flew over the arena with a sign advertising the LP trailing behind; it was pure show.
Some of the songs may be new, but they had the same tired old riffs. But with all the hand clapping and waving of Van Halen banners, it was obvious to all that these exponents of HM were the reason for the gathering of the clans; a Union Jack even stood high above the crowd.
So I may be a little bored with all this guitar thrashing but, credit where credit's due, there wasn't a person whose attention was distracted during Edward Van Halen's final guitar solo; and the version of the Kinks 'You Really Got Me' was a treat.
It's about 6.30 pm and the crowd is already thinning out (those damn trains, I guess). More's the pity, for Geleen is in for a rare treat; the J Geils Band. They're heavier and tighter than before, but they've not lost that base that gives them such pulling power. Lead singer Peter Wolfe prances about stage like there's no tomorrow, joined every so often by Magic Dick on some fine blues harp. His blowin' leads into a few choruses of 'Peachy Tree' before the band launch into the title track of their last album, 'Love Stinks'.
Judging by the cheering the crowd's just as pleased to hear a bit of good old rock 'n' roll as I am. Geils are a joy to watch; good musicianship, good times, all wrapped up in a parcel of fun. If there had been aisles then everyone would have danced in them.
Following that was a problem. The adrenalin was running high, but the crowds were thinning out. The Jam played a well-rehearsed, predictable set. Out came the message through numbers like 'Eton Rifles' and 'Going Underground', echoing the band's increasing commerciality.
But the Jam's vibrant crispness was less than was needed. A quick pick-me-up from the ashes of Van Halen and the J Geils Band was doomed from the start. From a sell-out British tour to a depleted Dutch audience into HM — it's a cruel world.
NIK OAKLEY

JOE JACKSON
Paris Studios, London.

THERE'S TWO ways you can look at this gig: either as a BBC 'In Concert' broadcast or a taster for the upcoming tour. While ostensibly the former, it deputised as the latter, showing Ol' Joe in barn - storming form, evidently unspoiled by recent chart hits, overseas success and all the other ingredients of his new - found fame.
Verily did he dash round the stage like a cat on hot bricks, blazing a trail 'twixt microphone and keyboards as he bellowed his way through a concise set of unadulterated beefiness.
Opening with 'Look Sharp', Jackson and his impossibly tight backing band did their damnedest to practise what they preach, immaculately clad in black and red, for a crowd comprising coach - loads of school kids.
Joe knows he ain't the best - looking dude on a West End stage, something which is having an effect on his song - writing. Nowhere is this more obvious than in a new number, 'Pretty Boys' which was appropriately followed by 'Don't Wanna Be Like That', whose chorus echoes that of the Rats' 'Looking After No 1', a curious reversal in the theft stakes if ever there was one.
Jackson has got such a chip on his shoulder that he sardonically referred to his fashionably effete guitarist, Gary Sanford, as “honky tonk!” Elsewhere, however, he showed a healthy respect for the group, magnanimously demanding that they be acknowledged as “musicians.”
Meanwhile, his asides to the audience are frequently as cynical as the lyrics themselves. The excellent 'Geraldine And John' was touchingly introduced as “a song that could bring a tear to a glass eye”, whilst Graham Maby's instrument conking out was greeted with the remark “I usually only have to apologise for the bass player — not his equipment as well!”
Needless to say, that bit was edited out of the broadcast, unlike the poppy 'Kinda Kute' which Joe wasn't slow to introduce as the next single. Then came a pleasant surprise in the form of Jimmy Cliff's 'The Harder They Come', with Dave Haughton's drums realistically reggaematic.
Then the pace quickened for a rousing 'I'm The Man', the man in question leaping around and mercilessly mauling what's left of his hair. Following a Ramonic ending complete with “Hey ho! let's go!”, we grudgingly did go, having received enough to whet the appetite but leave the stomach demanding more. In all, a satisfying snack which augurs well for the banquet of later dates. MIKE NICHOLLS

Joe Jackson : the life of the party
Joe Jackson
The Bottom Line
New York City,br>April 20th, 1979
By John Milward

SOMEONE AT THE Bottom Line shouts out a request for Elvis Costello’s “Watching the Detectives,” and Joe Jackson responds with a cool, uppity glare that seems to say there’s one in every crowd. This isn’t just New Wave belligerence, however; rather, it’s Jackson baring his competitive instincts. And his resentment is understandable, especially since his appeal so closely mirrors Costello’s. Both men write pithy, melodic songs that shuffle proven pop styles like so many playing cards. But where Costello’s angry lyrics distance him from the crowd, Jackson sticks to the more traditional themes of romance and the advantages therein of “looking sharp.” Costello seeks to be the fly in the ointment; Jackson wants to be the life of the party.
Jackson opened the second of four sold-out Bottom Line shows with “One More Time,” and the song’s Who-cum-Kinks construction came on like a battle cry for another British invasion. Echoes of other old masters appeared throughout the set, from the bleating mannerisms of the Dave Clark Five (“Throw It Away”) to the low-smack charm of the early Beatles (the chorus to “Is She Really Going Out with Him?”). But Jackson is a talented thief, and the obvious influences can’t keep his good songs down.
Guitarist Gary Sanford is the sharpest of the power trio that backs Jackson, with his torrent of tightly choked chords pushing the singer’s cheap organ and giving the songs a feverish electric edge. The rhythm section, however, can be a bit sluggish; the band sometimes sounds as if it were chasing the arrangement instead of standing squarely on top of it. But experience should tighten Jackson’s act; Elvis Costello and the Attractions’ first two American tours were as different as night and day, and we should expect no less from Joe Jackson.
Though his lean-bones style and close-cropped hair put him squarely in the postpunk pop camp, his onstage personality is old-school ego. His patter was uncomfortably one-dimensional: he boasted about his hitbound chart position, asked who had bought his Look Sharp! LP and introduced a mediocre, sincere cover of Toots and the Maytals’ “Pressure Drop” as the “real” source of the reggae standard. When he introduced his song of media myopia, “Sunday Papers,” he quoted headlines from an easy target, the National Enquirer, instead of, say, the Sunday New York Times.
Joe Jackson is compatible with the other classically styled, commercially successful bands that have grown from the New Wave’s soil (e.g., the Police, Cars). The bold line on Jackson is that the mainstream AOR acceptance of his relatively low-key cabaret rock reads people to more adventurous New Wave performers like the Clash. This analysis standard-fails on experience, however; isn’t AOR as strong as Jackson’s best tunes. Jackson must yet prove that he will go deeper than his floor-plan pop framework, but his splashing debut has set an admirably high standard.

JOE JACKSON
London Nashville
IF IAN Dury is the Max Miller of rock'n'roll, then Joe Jackson is probably the Max Bygraves.
The music hall ingredients are obvious: 'cheekie chappie' patter, limp wrist, pink face, striped suit, winning smile. All of which might sound like gimmickry. But it isn't.
Or even if it is, it's done with such genuine affection and skill that it matters not all. The important thing is that Joe Jackson has the presence to carry it off. He has style, precious and elegant.
But for Jackson – as for Dury – sartorial sass is just the icing on a musically rich cake.
He has an instinctive grasp for his ragged-edged pop songs, and a peculiarly unique, tough-and-and-tender voice. Commercial without being wet, rooted in sixties feel but nothing if not the sound of 1978.
He and the band don't really sound like anyone, but visually there are several remarkable doppelgangers. Guitarist Gary Sanford bears a disconcerting resemblance to Mickey Most. Drummer Dave Houghton looks like Bun E. Carlos of Cheap Trick and Joe himself is a peculiar hybrid of Bygraves and Peter Skellern.
Maybe to look at they're a walking waxworks, but musically they're a great deal more animate than anything Madame Tussaud could dream up. Jackson contorts and stiffens agonizingly, while Sanford contents himself with pursuing Joe around the stage with his guitar.
Jackson sticks to no firm line of policy on-stage; the material swings from the super hard reggae of 'Fools In Love' to the Steve Miller romantics of 'Is She Really Going Out With Him' and the frantic 'No Time To Lose'.
He is no avant-garde doyen, no barrier-cracking experimentalist; all the songs are basically conservative – even to the extent of Joe performing a version of Fats Waller's 'Ain't Misbehavin''.
But he has elan, charm, talent and a very nice suit. He will Hit Big soon. That prediction is official.
TIM LOTT

NOTE: Joe Jackson – Never A Dull Moment by Ron Young (photo by Robbin Cresswell) Amidst all the heavy metal rock sounds of bands like Judas Priest, Van Halen and Riot that are heard daily on KISS/KMAC program director Lou Roney will occasionally play something by Joe Jackson. Jackson's music is sharp and direct. It's streamlined, stripped-down rock 'n' roll that is propelled by his two-edged blade of a voice. His songs are about real life—not some rock 'n' roll fantasy—and his lyrics cut to the bone. While some listeners may think that Joe Jackson is just an Elivs-Costello soundalike they've got another think coming. "I feel that the press has blown the Elvis-Costello comparison out of proportion. I wish they'd fucking shut up about it," Jackson rants after his dynamite performance at Austin's Armadillo World Headquarters. "When people compare me to Elvis I think, 'Aww shit'. But when they compare me to Graham Parker, whom I like alot, I think that's quite flattering because at least Parker's very genuine." If there are comaprisons to be made at all between Jackson and Costello one would have to mention that both have English Pub Rock roots and that each write songs that deal with the problems of lost love and the frustrating search for it. But while Elvis may twist people and situations to fit his own reality Jackson's songs are more down to earth. "Elvis is always trying to be so clever and I'm not trying to do that. I'm trying to write something that has real meaning to me and not about fantasies but real life. I write songs that everyone can identify with," Jackson says leaning back in chair and easing off his shoes. A picture of Joe Jackson in concert is one of a whirling dervish of a young man bouncing about the stage putting his three-piece band through their paces. Letting loose all his pent-up energies and emotions, but like a good actor making it all look easy. (Jackson, in fact, the following night in Houston broke his foot after jumping from atop his piano while ending his performance.). "I try to communicate with people, that's what I'm up there for. I want the band to come across like a band that I would want to see. Like if I see a performer who gives the impression that they don't give a shit about me, the audience, then I feel cheated and I don't like it. They're performing for themselves and they don't really care. I think you should feel that the performer is trying to say something to you, otherwise what's the point. That's another reason why I'm fed up being compared to Elvis because he's sort of arrogant in his stage show and I don't relate to it." Jackson enrolled at the Royal Academy of Music in London where he studied percusssion and piano. "I don't know what I was doing there really ... wasting my time basically. During the three years I was there though I hardly ever showed my face because I was writing and playing in bands. Mostly bands tha tplayed Top-50 stuff ... like cover versions of other people's songs. I worked around in clubs and then I sort of graduated to playing more and more original material. So by the time I left college I was in a band that was playing all original materical. That band was called Arms and Legs and we eventually got a recording contract and put three singles out. It was for MAM Records in England who had Gilbert O'Sullivan. But they just sort of put the singles out and didn't promote them. We didn't have proper equipment to go on the road, no finance or anything. I was just shit and a waste of time really." A&M Records is the label he eventually signed with. They believe in Joe Jackson. They're paying for his U.S. tour and they're promoting him like crazy. His first album Look Sharp (which are songs from his original demo tapes) was number 61 on Billboard's charts at this writing. But before Jackson ended up at A&M he had been turned down by Stiff Records, the spawning ground for Ian Dury, Nick Lowe and Elvis Costello himself. "Well, Stiff is a nice little club where everyone fits in and I didn't fit in," he says with some bitterness. "The official story is that they sent me a very nice letter actually which said that 'We like your tape but don't see it as Stiff material, however we feel sure you'll get there.' Which I did. (laughs) But Stiff wasn't really the right label for me. I was rejected by Virgin Records too which doesn't bother me either. I think I ended up with the best company for what I'm doing, especially from the viewpoint of the States. "Before the deal with A&M I got the guys in the band together (Gary Sanford on guitar, Graham Maby on bass and Dave Houghton on drums), all of whom I've known for years, to do an album's worth of material. At that time the band was jsut friends of mine and I sort of used them as session musicians if you like. But when there became a possibility of arecording deal they were hovering around and ... We've become more of a band now since we've been playing together now for a year. Anyway then I began to take the master tapes round to all the record companies trying to get a release on it. So in effect I was my own production company. If no one had picked me up I would've gotten the album pressed myself to attract attention. I would have gotten it out one way or another," Jackson emphatically states. On Joe Jackson's debut album Look Sharp a shiny new pair of white Winklepicker shoes beneath black drainpipe trousers are what catch the eye in the record bins. It's an image that says he's a smart dresser and that he's street smart too. An image that's as meticulously crafted as his power-pop songs. But it's also a watch word that tells you to be aware of what goes on around you and to know where your're going. Just like Joe Jackson.

Pretty Girls, Look Sharp!, Baby Stick Around, Is She Really Going Out With Him?, Got the Time, One More Time, Sunday Papers, Ain't Misbehavin', Fools in Love, Come On, Ain't That a Shame
NOTE: Joe Jackson Hope and Anchor There's talent, and there's talent. Joe Jackson has both. His single "Is She Really Going Out With Him" is playing on tape. Survivors of the weather conditions are singing along in a state of partial thaw. A Scotsman informs me that "JJ's dead brilliant." I mention his name to the bar staff, and they lapse into starry-eyed ecstasy. Is it a conspiracy? The band arrive to a heartwarming reception. Drummer Dave Houghton wears black, guitarist Gary Sanford wears white, bassman Graham Maybe wears both, and the man himself favours a hoodlum pin-stripe with a gross-out polkadot tie. He looks like he hasn't slept for a month; he acts like he doesn't need to. First impressions of the set suggest an excellence in every respect; from then on it only improves. A near-perfect sound balance points out the most thoughtful, controlled springboard backing, the band's range widened by their deliberately economic style. Over this, Joe's precision lyrics paint a very clear picture; an unusually sharp mix of observation and sentiment given an added lift by his confidential cabaret-type delivery. Pacing throughout is supreme. "Pretty Girls", "Look Sharp" and "Baby Stick Around" are all firmly grounded in slick, dance band rock. There's the same clipped, tense appeal as Costello, but with an immediate warmth and colour. Shuffled into a mostly fast moving set are a couple of reggae-based numbers. The first, "Sunday Papers" makes the same stab at the tabloids as The Jam's "News Of The World". More acute, and less a statement of the obvious, it comes with a killer chorus line and a dedication to the overhyped news feature of the week: Todd Rundgren's codpiece. The second is "Fools In Love", a shamelessly catchy and lilting song that's almost a ballad. So much so, that if it were to fall into alien hands it would probably resurface with palmcourt orchestration. As it stand it's unique, both for a lyric that strangely alternates sleaze and aggression, and the uncannily thin dub rhythm that traces out the vocal line. Also on offer is a genuinely affectionate version of Fats Waller's "Ain't Misbehavin'". Busking most of the lyrics, Joe plays it as a keyboard solo, which shows an evident technical skill that will allow him endless possibilities with the band. Joined for three encores by Ian Gomm, they play Domino and Chuck Berry covers "Ain't That A Shame" and "Come On". Not a gratuitous, fail-safe exit route, but two fine re-vamped versions that finally spotlight Sanford's solos. '79 will see an ascent of the charts by Joe Jackson. You'll believe a man can fly. Mark Ellen
The very first performance of "I´m the Man" (according to concert review)

Joe Jackson Leeds The eight-foot-six Neurotic Stockbroker look just had to reckon sooner or later, but even though he's been squaring-off all his life, spiv rocker Joe Jackson now has the kind of image which not even a seasoned actor could contrive. Cabaret in Portsmouth must do something for a man. In the case of Jackson, more has been revived than the polka dot. Keeled over and automatically combing his hair on the condensation stalactites which have a tendency to proliferate at the Fan Club on nights like this, Jackson spewed his vitriolic raps over an audience of punters barely ready for the pin-striped phenomenon who sweated, swigged pils and executed open-heart surgery for their perusal. 'One More Time', a sure-fire opener sung in sure-fire manic style (cf. Graham Parker) paved the way here for a brutally fast-moving 50-minute set which easily trashed the Leeds all-comers' record. Fronting a band whose frugality more or less defines 'minimalism', contender Jackson gets through his fair share of hang-ups in a gig, but nothing here (not even a hiccupping fire siren) could prevent him from getting everything out of his system. Spoken preambles spotlighted the humourist communicator in Jackson: "I quit the polka dots (for horizontal stripes) because the NME don't like them. I wouldn't know what to wear if it wasn't for them," while the keen, terse lyrics of 'Is She Really Going Out With Him?' (cf. Steve Miller), dedicated to Rick Nielsen and Cheap Trick who he'd just seen up the road, 'Look Sharp', 'Fools In Love' and (hey Joe, what you doin' with that pun?) 'Happy Loving Couples' (cf. Elvis Costello) ensured that nobody left thinking Jackson was just a joker. The unrecorded 'I'm The Man' promised even more, possessing a similar intensity to the 'Look Sharp' collection, but with a much more obviously commercial structure and feel — and featuring a vocal fade-out which one dares Jackson to record: "I was last year's model, baby, and I'm going to be next year's too." Very camp, very cocky. But still cool. Introducing the band "because they're so good," Jackson gives credit where due. Pirouetting and generally flipping out behind him, guitarist Gary Sanford and bassist Graham Maby provide a complementary bizarrerie as an oddball backdrop to Jacko's frenzied stoicism. The no-superfluous-action 3-D vista is competitive, especially if and when you could also see drummer Dave Houghton — a physical impossibility not exclusive to myself. Jackson's raw harp (featuring prominently on 'The Fever', the flip of the single) and boogie electric piano (notably on 'Ain't That A Shame') were successful, if a little gratuitous. They seemed conclusive indications that Jackson (unwisely?) intends to take the scope of his talents to the outer reaches of endless possibility. But essentially, Jackson knows where he's going (you can't put a good spiv down) and hopefully, most similarities with other rock artistes past, present, living or dead, are subconscious rip-offs. They told you J.J. was going to be BIG, and you suckers, you believed them. This time around, though, nobody loses. If Jackson has seemed to fall into the 'hype' bracket, then this at least is one hype we can all use. Emma Ruth
